stages.name: No Punic coinage
stages.desc: No Punic mint, and Punic coins rare or absent

stages.name: Punic coins in circulation
stages.desc: Carthaginian coins used, but not struck, here

stages.name: Active Punic mint
stages.desc: Carthage or a Punic city strikes coins here

stages.name: Lost to Rome
stages.desc: A former Punic mint or coin zone now under Roman rule

states.name: Spain
timeline: Gadir and the Punic towns of the south trade without coins of their own
Gadir strikes coins with tuna; Ibiza (Ebusus) strikes bronze with the god Bes
Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir: Barcid silver from the Spanish mines
Hasdrubal founds Carthago Nova, the Barcids' capital and mint
Scipio storms Carthago Nova; Gadir and Ibiza still mint
After Ilipa, Gadir goes over to Rome; Punic Spain is lost

states.name: Libya
timeline: Greek Cyrene mints its own silver; the Punic towns of the Syrtis strike none
Carthaginian coins circulate in Lepcis, Oea and Sabratha
Masinissa seizes the Emporia from Carthage

states.name: Tunisia
timeline: Carthage trades in weighed silver and credit; its first coins are struck for Sicily
The Carthage mint opens: gold, electrum and bronze (date disputed)
Agathocles invades Africa; the electrum grows paler
Regulus invades: pure gold is struck in haste
The Mercenary War: Libyan rebels strike their own coins
The revolt is crushed; Carthage mints near-pure gold again
War coinage: silver debased with copper and lead
After Zama: bronze only, some pieces of a hundred grams
Under siege, Carthage strikes its last gold, silver and bronze
Carthage is destroyed; its land becomes the Roman province of Africa

states.name: Italy
timeline: Sicily: Carthage strikes horse-and-palm silver to pay its army; Motya and Panormus also mint
Dionysius of Syracuse destroys Motya; Lilybaeum replaces it the next year
New silver with a female head and standing horse pays for the war against Timoleon
Sicilian silver names 'the paymasters'; Punic mints in Sardinia strike bronze
Defeat off the Aegates Islands: Sicily is ceded to Rome; Sardinia still mints
Rome seizes Sardinia; Punic minting in Sicily and Sardinia ends
Coins for Hannibal's army in Bruttium; a last Punic issue for the Sardinian revolt
A Punic army in Sicily strikes silver over captured Roman denarii
Agrigentum falls to Rome; Hannibal's mints in the south carry on
Hannibal leaves Italy; no Punic mint remains

states.name: Algeria
timeline: Numidian kingdoms and Punic ports along the coast; no coinage
Carthaginian bronze circulates in the coastal ports and Numidian lands
Masinissa becomes king of Numidia; he will strike bronze with Punic letters

states.name: Malta
timeline: Punic towns on Malta and Gozo; no coins struck or in common use
Carthaginian and Siculo-Punic bronze circulate on the islands
Rome takes Malta at the start of the Second Punic War

events.title: Segesta asks for help
events.text: The Elymian city of Segesta, at war with Selinus, appeals to Carthage.

events.title: The first tetradrachms
events.text: Horse forepart and date palm, with the words 'Carthage' and 'the camp': silver to pay the army (410 or 409; mint disputed).

events.title: Selinus falls
events.text: Hannibal Mago's army storms Selinus after a nine-day siege.

events.title: Himera destroyed
events.text: Hannibal Mago razes Himera, where his grandfather had been defeated in 480.

events.title: Akragas sacked
events.text: Akragas falls after an eight-month siege; a Punic tetradrachm overstruck on its coin helps date the series.

events.title: Motya destroyed
events.text: Dionysius of Syracuse takes the island city of Motya, a Punic mint.

events.title: Lilybaeum founded
events.text: Survivors of Motya settle Lilybaeum, later a centre of Punic minting.

events.title: Siege of Syracuse
events.text: Himilco's siege of Syracuse collapses when plague strikes his camp.

events.title: Gold at Carthage
events.text: Carthage strikes gold and electrum at home, c. 350 by Jenkins and Lewis; Visonà dates the mint's start differently.

events.title: Battle of the Crimisus
events.text: Timoleon of Corinth defeats a Carthaginian army in western Sicily.

events.title: 'People of the camp'
events.text: New Sicilian silver names 'the people of the camp', as war with Agathocles begins.

events.title: Agathocles in Africa
events.text: Agathocles of Syracuse lands in Africa; Carthage's electrum falls to about 70% gold.

events.title: Gadir mints
events.text: Gadir, beyond the straits, begins striking coins with tuna fish.

events.title: Ibiza mints
events.text: Ebusus strikes bronze showing the god Bes.

events.title: Sardinian bronze
events.text: Punic mints in Sardinia strike bronze with Tanit and a horse.

events.title: Pyrrhus at Lilybaeum
events.text: Pyrrhus of Epirus overruns Punic Sicily but fails to take Lilybaeum.

events.title: War over Messana
events.text: A quarrel over Messana brings Rome and Carthage to war.

events.title: Regulus invades
events.text: As Regulus lands in Africa, Carthage strikes pure gold from hastily made iron dies.

events.title: Regulus defeated
events.text: The Spartan mercenary Xanthippus defeats Regulus near Tunis.

events.title: Aegates Islands
events.text: Rome's fleet wins; Carthage cedes Sicily and owes 3,200 talents.

events.title: Mercenaries at Sicca
events.text: More than 20,000 mercenaries back from Sicily demand their pay.

events.title: Coins 'of the Libyans'
events.text: The rebels strike silver marked ΛΙΒΥΩΝ, often over Carthage's own coins.

events.title: Rome seizes Sardinia
events.text: Rome takes Sardinia after its mercenary garrison revolts.

events.title: Revolt crushed
events.text: Hamilcar Barca destroys the rebel armies; Mathos is executed at Carthage.

events.title: Hamilcar in Spain
events.text: Hamilcar Barca lands at Gadir and begins a Punic realm in Spain.

events.title: Carthago Nova
events.text: Hasdrubal founds Qart Hadasht, 'New City', on a fine harbour.

events.title: Hannibal commands
events.text: Hannibal takes command in Spain; Pliny says one mine gave him 300 pounds of silver a day.

events.title: Siege of Saguntum
events.text: Hannibal takes Saguntum, Rome's ally, after eight months.

events.title: Rome takes Malta
events.text: A Roman fleet seizes Malta and its Punic garrison.

events.title: Over the Alps
events.text: Hannibal crosses the Alps into Italy.

events.title: Cannae
events.text: Hannibal destroys a Roman army at Cannae.

events.title: Sardinian revolt
events.text: Hampsicora's revolt brings a Punic army and a last Punic issue to Sardinia.

events.title: Hannibal's mints
events.text: Gold-silver pieces for Hannibal's army in Bruttium (some scholars say Capua).

events.title: Tarentum
events.text: Hannibal takes Tarentum, which strikes coins on a Punic standard.

events.title: Agrigentum falls
events.text: Rome retakes Agrigentum, probably the mint of Punic silver struck over Roman coins.

events.title: Carthago Nova falls
events.text: Scipio storms the Barcid capital and its mint.

events.title: Gadir goes over
events.text: After Ilipa, Gadir surrenders to Rome; Punic Spain is lost.

events.title: Hannibal leaves Italy
events.text: Recalled to Africa, Hannibal sails from Croton.

events.title: Zama
events.text: Scipio defeats Hannibal at Zama.

events.title: 10,000 talents
events.text: Peace: Carthage must pay 10,000 talents of silver over fifty years.

events.title: Debt paid early?
events.text: Carthage offers to pay its whole indemnity at once; Rome refuses.

events.title: Masinissa takes Emporia
events.text: The Numidian king seizes Carthage's towns on the Syrtis coast.

events.title: Third Punic War
events.text: Rome declares war; besieged Carthage strikes its last coins.

events.title: Carthage destroyed
events.text: Scipio Aemilianus takes the city; survivors are sold into slavery.

chartNote: Share of the area of six present-day countries, by Punic minting activity. Regions are today's boundaries: Italy stands for Sicily and Sardinia, Spain for the Punic south and Ibiza, Libya for Tripolitania; the vast Algerian and Libyan interiors swing the shares. A simplification: mints opened and closed town by town, and many dates rest on hoards and die studies that are disputed.
